1.summary: Mark opens with John the Baptizer and Jesus' baptism and testing, then shows Jesus calling fishermen, teaching with authority in Capernaum, healing the sick and a leper, and preaching through Galilee.
1.lookfor: Notice how fast the story moves, Jesus' first words, and whom he tells to keep quiet.

names.name: Nazareth
names.gloss: Jesus' home village in Galilee.

names.name: Andrew
names.gloss: A fisherman, Simon's brother.

names.name: Zebedee
names.gloss: A fisherman with hired servants, father of James and John.

names.name: Capernaum
names.gloss: A town on the north shore of the Sea of Galilee.

insights.title: Good News
insights.body: Mark's first line, "The beginning of the Good News of Jesus Christ, the Son of God" (1:1), uses euangelion. In the Roman world the word announced events such as an emperor's birthday or a victory. Isaiah used the related Hebrew word for news of God's reign.

insights.title: Immediately
insights.body: Mark uses the Greek euthys, immediately, more than forty times, and it appears again and again in this chapter (1:10, 1:12, 1:18). The effect is breathless. Jesus' work moves with urgency.

insights.title: Three prophets in one
insights.body: Mark says "As it is written in the prophets" (1:2), as the WEB follows; many manuscripts read in Isaiah the prophet. The quotation blends Malachi and Exodus with Isaiah 40. The messenger prepares the way for the Lord himself.

insights.title: With the wild animals
insights.body: Only Mark mentions that Jesus was "with the wild animals" (1:13). Some see danger; others a picture of peace with creation, like Isaiah's vision or Adam among the animals. Either way, angels serve him there.

insights.title: The time is fulfilled
insights.body: Jesus' first words sum up his message: "The time is fulfilled, and God's Kingdom is at hand! Repent, and believe in the Good News." (1:15). The word for time, kairos, means the decisive moment. What the prophets waited for has arrived.

insights.title: Silencing the demons
insights.body: Jesus silences demons who know who he is (1:25, 1:34) and tells the healed leper to say nothing (1:44). Scholars call this Mark's messianic secret. Jesus avoids titles that would be taken as a political Messiah until his suffering shows what kind of king he is.

insights.title: The synagogue at Capernaum
insights.body: Visitors to Capernaum see a white limestone synagogue from about the fourth or fifth century, built on dark basalt foundations that many think belong to the synagogue of Jesus' day (1:21). A house venerated by early Christians as Peter's lies a short walk away (1:29).

insights.title: Early in the morning
insights.body: Even when "Everyone is looking for you" (1:37), Jesus slips away in the dark to pray alone (1:35). What crowds out your time alone with God?

2.summary: Jesus forgives and heals a paralysed man lowered through a roof, calls Levi and eats with tax collectors, answers a question about fasting, and defends his disciples for picking grain on the Sabbath.
2.lookfor: Notice the four friends' faith, each question Jesus' critics ask, and the saying about the Sabbath found only in Mark.

names.name: Capernaum
names.gloss: Jesus' home base in Galilee.

names.name: Levi
names.gloss: A tax collector, called Matthew in Matthew's Gospel.

names.name: Alphaeus
names.gloss: Levi's father.

names.name: Abiathar
names.gloss: A priest in David's time, later high priest.

insights.title: Through the roof
insights.body: Houses in Capernaum had flat roofs of beams, branches and packed clay, reached by an outside stair (2:4). Digging through was possible and could be repaired. Jesus calls the friends' persistence faith (2:5).

insights.title: Who can forgive?
insights.body: The scribes ask, "Who can forgive sins but God alone?" (2:7). They are right in principle, and that is the point. Jesus' answer claims a right that belongs to God (2:10).

insights.title: Son of Man
insights.body: This is the first time Jesus calls himself the Son of Man in Mark (2:10). The phrase was not a fixed political label, yet in Daniel a son of man receives authority from God. In Mark it gathers three ideas: present authority, coming suffering and future glory.

insights.title: Levi's dinner
insights.body: Jesus calls Levi from his tax booth (2:14), and Levi hosts a meal where "many tax collectors and sinners" eat with Jesus (2:15). Sharing a table meant acceptance. Jesus explains that the sick are the ones who need a doctor (2:17).

insights.title: Groomsmen don't fast
insights.body: Wedding guests were excused from religious fasting during the week of celebration (2:19). Jesus pictures his presence as a wedding. The bridegroom "will be taken away" (2:20) is the first hint of his death in Mark.

insights.title: Abiathar or Ahimelech?
insights.body: Jesus says David ate the holy bread "at the time of Abiathar the high priest" (2:26), but 1 Samuel names Ahimelech, Abiathar's father. Suggested explanations include that the phrase means in the passage about Abiathar, or that Abiathar was present and became better known. Matthew and Luke leave the name out.

insights.title: Made for people
insights.body: Only Mark records, "The Sabbath was made for man, not man for the Sabbath" (2:27). Some rabbis taught something similar, that the Sabbath was given to people and not people to the Sabbath. It was a gift of rest from creation, not a burden.

3.summary: Jesus heals a withered hand on the Sabbath, crowds come from far away, he appoints the Twelve, his family thinks he has lost his mind, and he answers the charge that he works by Beelzebul.
3.lookfor: Notice Jesus' emotions, how the family scenes frame the dispute with the scribes, and who Jesus calls his family.

names.name: Herodians
names.gloss: Supporters of Herod Antipas.

names.name: Idumaea
names.gloss: The old land of Edom, south of Judea.

names.name: Thaddaeus
names.gloss: One of the Twelve.

names.name: Judas Iscariot
names.gloss: The disciple who betrayed Jesus.

names.name: Beelzebul
names.gloss: A name for the prince of demons.

insights.title: Anger and grief
insights.body: Only Mark says Jesus looked around "with anger, being grieved at the hardening of their hearts" (3:5). Mark shows Jesus' emotions more openly than the other Gospels. His anger is at hard hearts, not at the man in need.

insights.title: An early plot
insights.body: Already in chapter 3, Pharisees and Herodians plan to destroy him (3:6). The Herodians backed Herod Antipas, the ruler who would kill John. The shadow of the cross falls early in Mark.

insights.title: From Idumaea to Sidon
insights.body: Crowds come from Idumaea in the far south, from beyond the Jordan, and from around Tyre and Sidon in the north (3:8). Idumaea was the old Edom, the homeland of Herod's family. People from Gentile regions are already drawn to him.

insights.title: To be with him
insights.body: Jesus appoints twelve "that they might be with him" (3:14), and only then to be sent out. Being with him comes before working for him. Mark's list, like Matthew's, includes Thaddaeus.

insights.title: Sons of Thunder
insights.body: Jesus nicknames James and John Boanerges, "Sons of Thunder" (3:17), perhaps for their fiery temper. Luke tells how they once wanted to call down fire on a Samaritan village. The Aramaic behind the name is debated.

insights.title: He is insane
insights.body: Jesus' own family set out to seize him, saying, "He is insane" (3:21). Mark places the scribes' charge of Beelzebul (3:22-30) between the family setting out and arriving (3:31). Both misjudge him, one out of worry and one out of hostility; this sandwiching is typical of Mark.

insights.title: Binding the strong man
insights.body: Jesus' picture of tying up the strong man (3:27) presents his exorcisms as the defeat of Satan's rule. It echoes Isaiah's promise that captives will be taken from the mighty. The kingdom comes as a rescue.

insights.title: Those around him
insights.body: Jesus looks at those sitting around him and calls them his mother and brothers (3:34-35). Who would he point to around you?

4.summary: Jesus teaches parables by the sea: the sower, the lamp, the seed that grows by itself and the mustard seed; then he calms a storm that terrifies his disciples.
4.lookfor: Notice how often Jesus talks about hearing, the parable found only in Mark, and the disciples' question at the end.

insights.title: Listen!
insights.body: The parable begins with "Listen!" (4:3) and ends with "Whoever has ears to hear, let him hear" (4:9). Later Jesus says, "Take heed what you hear" (4:24). The whole chapter is about hearing well, as Israel's great prayer begins, Hear, Israel.

insights.title: So that they may not perceive?
insights.body: Mark 4:12 sounds as if parables are meant to keep people out. Jesus quotes Isaiah's call, where the prophet's preaching hardens those who refuse. Parables divide hearers: those who come close and ask receive more (4:10, 4:34).

insights.title: Mystery
insights.body: "To you is given the mystery of God's Kingdom" (4:11). In the New Testament mysterion means a secret now revealed by God, not a puzzle. The secret is that the kingdom has come in Jesus, hidden in weakness.

insights.title: Seed growing secretly
insights.body: Only Mark has the parable of seed that grows while the farmer sleeps, "though he doesn't know how" (4:27). God gives the growth; the sower's part is to sow and to wait. Paul says the same about ministry.

insights.title: The cushion in the stern
insights.body: Fishing boats had a steering oar in the stern and a seat or cushion for the helmsman (4:38). A first-century boat found in the mud of the Sea of Galilee in 1986 is about eight metres long, the kind of boat the disciples may have used.

insights.title: Don't you care?
insights.body: The disciples' words are sharp: "Teacher, don't you care that we are dying?" (4:38). Matthew and Luke soften them. Mark keeps the disciples' raw fear and their failures throughout his Gospel.

insights.title: Who then is this?
insights.body: Jesus speaks to the sea, "Peace! Be still!" (4:39), using the Greek word for be muzzled that he used to silence a demon in chapter 1. In the Old Testament only God rules the sea. The disciples end more afraid than before (4:41).

insights.title: Which soil?
insights.body: The same seed meets very different ground (4:14-20). Which kind of soil best describes how you are hearing right now?

5.summary: Across the lake Jesus frees a man possessed by a legion of demons, and back on the other side he heals a woman who touches his clothes and raises the daughter of Jairus, a synagogue ruler.
5.lookfor: Notice the three requests in the first story, how the second story interrupts the third, and the Aramaic words Jesus speaks.

names.name: Gadarenes
names.gloss: People of the region of Gadara, east of the Sea of Galilee.

names.name: Legion
names.gloss: The name the demons give themselves.

names.name: Decapolis
names.gloss: Ten Greek-speaking cities, mostly east of the Jordan.

names.name: Jairus
names.gloss: A leader of a synagogue.

insights.title: Among the tombs
insights.body: The man lives among tombs (5:3), in Gentile country, near a herd of pigs. Everything about the scene was unclean by Jewish standards. Jesus walks straight into it.

insights.title: Legion
insights.body: A Roman legion had around five thousand soldiers (5:9). The name suggests overwhelming numbers. Some see a hint at Roman occupation, since a legion stationed in the region later used a boar as its emblem.

insights.title: Three requests
insights.body: Three parties beg Jesus here: the demons to enter the pigs (5:12), the townspeople for him to leave (5:17), and the healed man to go with him (5:18). Jesus grants the first two and refuses the third. He sends the man home to tell what the Lord has done (5:19).

insights.title: A witness in the Decapolis
insights.body: The man proclaims in the Decapolis what Jesus has done (5:20). In Gentile territory, with less risk of political misunderstanding, Jesus does not ask for silence. When Jesus returns to the Decapolis, people bring the sick to him.

insights.title: Twelve years
insights.body: The woman has bled for twelve years, as long as Jairus's daughter has lived (5:25, 5:42). Her condition made her ritually unclean, and she had spent everything on doctors (5:26). Luke, traditionally a physician, leaves out the remark that the doctors made her worse.

insights.title: One story inside another
insights.body: Jairus's urgent request is interrupted by the woman's healing (5:21-43), another of Mark's sandwiches. The delay seems disastrous, yet both stories are about faith facing fear. Jesus tells Jairus, "Don't be afraid, only believe" (5:36).

insights.title: Talitha cumi
insights.body: Mark keeps Jesus' Aramaic words, "Talitha cumi!" (5:41), little girl, get up. Mark preserves Jesus' own Aramaic more than any other Gospel, perhaps from Peter's memory. Peter was one of the three allowed in the room (5:37).

insights.title: Who touched me?
insights.body: In a pressing crowd Jesus stops for one woman (5:30-34) and calls her "Daughter". What would it mean to you to be noticed like that?

6.summary: Jesus is rejected at Nazareth and sends out the Twelve; Herod has John the Baptizer beheaded; Jesus feeds five thousand and walks on the water to his struggling disciples.
6.lookfor: Notice what Jesus' home town calls him, Herod's mixed feelings about John, and what the disciples fail to understand.

names.name: Joses
names.gloss: One of Jesus' brothers.

names.name: Judah
names.gloss: One of Jesus' brothers, also called Judas or Jude.

names.name: Herod
names.gloss: Herod Antipas, ruler of Galilee.

names.name: Herodias
names.gloss: Herod's wife, formerly married to his half-brother.

names.name: Bethsaida
names.gloss: A fishing town at the north end of the lake.

names.name: Gennesaret
names.gloss: A plain on the north-west shore of the lake.

insights.title: The carpenter, son of Mary
insights.body: Only Mark calls Jesus himself "the carpenter, the son of Mary" (6:3). Naming a man by his mother was unusual and may reflect that Joseph had died, or gossip about his birth. Matthew has the carpenter's son.

insights.title: No mighty work there
insights.body: Mark says Jesus "could do no mighty work there" except heal a few sick people (6:5). Faith is not the power behind miracles, but unbelief shuts people off from what Jesus offers. He "marveled because of their unbelief" (6:6).

insights.title: Two by two
insights.body: The Twelve go out in pairs (6:7), matching the law's requirement of two witnesses. They travel light, with staff and sandals, as Israel was told to be dressed at the first Passover. Hospitality would supply the rest (6:10).

insights.title: Anointing the sick
insights.body: The disciples anoint the sick with oil and heal them (6:13); olive oil was common medicine. James later tells church elders to anoint the sick and pray. Catholic and Orthodox Christians see here a root of the sacrament of anointing of the sick.

insights.title: Herod heard him gladly
insights.body: Mark alone describes Herod's fascination with John: he feared him, kept him safe and "heard him gladly" (6:20). Yet the ruler who listened to a prophet killed him rather than lose face before his guests (6:26).

insights.title: Sheep without a shepherd
insights.body: Jesus has compassion because the crowd is "like sheep without a shepherd" (6:34). He has them sit in groups "on the green grass" (6:39), recalling the green pastures of Psalm 23. Ezekiel promised that God himself would shepherd his flock.

insights.title: He would have passed by
insights.body: Walking on the sea, Jesus "would have passed by them" (6:48). The Greek Old Testament uses the same verb when God passes by Moses and Elijah to show his glory. It may be a revelation, not indifference.

insights.title: Hardened hearts
insights.body: Mark ends with a surprise: "they hadn't understood about the loaves, but their hearts were hardened" (6:52). Not only opponents but the disciples struggle to see. Mark's honesty about them may have encouraged readers who also struggled.

7.summary: Jesus challenges the Pharisees' tradition of hand-washing and teaches that defilement comes from the heart, heals the daughter of a Syrophoenician woman, and opens the ears of a deaf man in the Decapolis.
7.lookfor: Notice where Mark stops to explain customs, the word "first" in Jesus' reply to the woman, and how he heals the deaf man.

names.name: Pharisees
names.gloss: Teachers devoted to the law and its traditions.

names.name: Tyre
names.gloss: A Gentile port city on the Phoenician coast.

names.name: Sidon
names.gloss: Another Phoenician port city.

names.name: Syrophoenician
names.gloss: A Phoenician from the Roman province of Syria.

names.name: Decapolis
names.gloss: A region of Greek-speaking cities.

insights.title: Mark explains
insights.body: Mark stops to explain Jewish washing customs (7:3-4), which suggests many of his readers were Gentiles who did not know them. He also translates Aramaic words. This fits the early tradition that he wrote for believers in Rome.

insights.title: Corban
insights.body: Corban is a Hebrew word for an offering dedicated to God (7:11). A vow of Corban could be used to block a son's duty to support his parents. Jesus says this makes God's word void through human tradition (7:13).

insights.title: All foods clean
insights.body: Mark adds that Jesus' teaching meant "purifying all foods" (7:19). This was a huge step for Jewish followers, and the early church struggled over it for years. Mark's comment reflects the settled view of his own church.

insights.title: Children first
insights.body: Jesus tells the Greek woman, "Let the children be filled first" (7:27). First implies that the Gentiles' turn will come. Her quick reply wins her request (7:29).

insights.title: Touch and spittle
insights.body: Jesus takes the deaf man aside and uses touch and saliva (7:33), signs a deaf man could understand. Saliva was widely thought to have healing power in the ancient world. Jesus looks up to heaven and sighs, as if in prayer (7:34).

insights.title: Ephphatha
insights.body: The Aramaic word "Ephphatha!" means be opened (7:34). The early church used it in baptism, when the minister touched the ears of the one being baptized. The Catholic baptism rite keeps it to this day.

insights.title: The deaf hear
insights.body: The crowd says, "He makes even the deaf hear, and the mute speak!" (7:37), echoing Isaiah's promise for the time God comes to save. The rare Greek word for the man's speech impediment (7:32) appears in the same passage of Isaiah in the Greek Old Testament.

8.summary: Jesus feeds four thousand, refuses to give a sign, warns about the yeast of the Pharisees and Herod, heals a blind man in two stages, receives Peter's confession, foretells his suffering, and calls his followers to take up their cross.
8.lookfor: Notice the questions Jesus fires at his disciples, the healing that comes in two stages, and how Peter reacts to talk of suffering.

names.name: Dalmanutha
names.gloss: An unknown place on the Sea of Galilee.

names.name: Herod
names.gloss: Herod Antipas, ruler of Galilee.

names.name: Bethsaida
names.gloss: A town at the north end of the lake.

names.name: Caesarea Philippi
names.gloss: A city at the foot of Mount Hermon.

insights.title: Dalmanutha
insights.body: Dalmanutha (8:10) is mentioned nowhere else, and its location is unknown. Matthew has Magdala in the same place in the story. Some think it was a spot near Magdala.

insights.title: Don't you understand yet?
insights.body: After two feedings, the disciples worry about having one loaf (8:16). Jesus fires questions at them (8:17-21) in the language Jeremiah used of a people with eyes that do not see. The section ends, "Don't you understand yet?" (8:21).

insights.title: Two-stage sight
insights.body: The blind man first sees people "like trees walking" (8:24), then clearly (8:25), the only healing in stages in the Gospels. Mark places it just before Peter's confession. Peter sees that Jesus is the Christ but not yet what kind of Christ.

insights.title: The hinge of the Gospel
insights.body: Near Caesarea Philippi, a city of pagan shrines and honours to Caesar, Jesus asks, "Who do men say that I am?" (8:27). Peter's answer in Mark is short: "You are the Christ" (8:29). From here the story turns toward Jerusalem.

insights.title: Must suffer
insights.body: Jesus teaches that the Son of Man "must suffer many things" (8:31). The Greek dei expresses necessity within God's plan, as Scripture foretold. Now he speaks "openly" (8:32).

insights.title: Seeing his disciples
insights.body: Jesus rebukes Peter while "seeing his disciples" (8:33), as if the correction is meant for them all. Peter has in mind the things of men. Then Jesus calls the crowd too, since the call to the cross is for everyone (8:34).

insights.title: Not ashamed
insights.body: Jesus warns that he will be ashamed of anyone ashamed of him "in this adulterous and sinful generation" (8:38). For Mark's first readers, facing persecution, this was no theory. Paul writes that he is not ashamed of the good news.

insights.title: What profit?
insights.body: "For what does it profit a man, to gain the whole world, and forfeit his life?" (8:36). What are you most tempted to gain at that price?

9.summary: Jesus is transfigured before three disciples, frees a boy from a spirit after the father cries out for help with his unbelief, again foretells his death, and teaches about greatness, welcome and the danger of causing others to stumble.
9.lookfor: Notice the move from the mountain to the crowd below, the father's honest prayer, and what the disciples argue about on the road.

names.name: Elijah
names.gloss: The prophet expected to return before the end.

names.name: Moses
names.gloss: The lawgiver.

names.name: Capernaum
names.gloss: Jesus' base in Galilee.

names.name: Gehenna
names.gloss: A name for the place of final judgment.

insights.title: No launderer could do it
insights.body: Mark says Jesus' clothes became whiter than any "launderer on earth can whiten them" (9:3), a homely touch typical of his vivid style. Peter "didn't know what to say" (9:6). Many see an eyewitness's memory behind such details.

insights.title: Elijah has come
insights.body: The disciples ask why Elijah must come first (9:11). Jesus says Elijah has come and was treated as people wished, "even as it is written about him" (9:13), meaning John the Baptizer. Elijah too had been hunted by a queen.

insights.title: Mountain and valley
insights.body: The glory on the mountain is followed at once by a suffering boy and helpless disciples below (9:14-18). Mark holds glory and suffering together. Raphael's last painting, The Transfiguration, puts both scenes in one picture.

insights.title: Help my unbelief
insights.body: The father cries, "I believe. Help my unbelief!" (9:24), and Jesus heals his son. Where is your faith mixed with doubt, and could you pray his prayer?

insights.title: Prayer and fasting
insights.body: Jesus says, "This kind can come out by nothing, except by prayer and fasting" (9:29). The words and fasting are missing from some of the oldest manuscripts. Either way the point is dependence on God rather than technique.

insights.title: A child in his arms
insights.body: While the disciples argue about who is greatest (9:34), Jesus sets a child among them and takes him in his arms (9:36). Children had no status in that world. To welcome such a one is to welcome Jesus and the Father who sent him (9:37).

insights.title: Not against us
insights.body: John tries to stop an outsider who casts out demons in Jesus' name (9:38). Jesus says, "For whoever is not against us is on our side" (9:40). Moses answered Joshua the same way when others prophesied outside the camp.

insights.title: Where their worm doesn't die
insights.body: The line "where their worm doesn't die, and the fire is not quenched" (9:48) is taken from the last verse of Isaiah. Gehenna was the valley of Hinnom, once a site of child sacrifice. The same line at verses 44 and 46 is missing from the oldest manuscripts.

10.summary: On the way to Jerusalem Jesus teaches about divorce, blesses children, tells a rich man to sell everything and follow him, foretells his death a third time, teaches that the greatest must serve, and gives sight to blind Bartimaeus.
10.lookfor: Notice Jesus' emotions, the question he asks two different people, and how the chapter ends on the road.

names.name: Judea
names.gloss: The southern region around Jerusalem.

names.name: Zebedee
names.gloss: Father of James and John.

names.name: Jericho
names.gloss: An oasis town on the road up to Jerusalem.

names.name: Timaeus
names.gloss: Father of Bartimaeus.

names.name: Bartimaeus
names.gloss: A blind beggar at Jericho; the name means son of Timaeus.

insights.title: Back to creation
insights.body: Jesus answers the question about divorce from Genesis (10:6-8). Moses' permission was given "For your hardness of heart" (10:5). Mark's version, unlike Matthew's, contains no exception clause.

insights.title: A wife who divorces
insights.body: Only Mark includes a wife divorcing her husband (10:12). Jewish law did not usually let a woman begin a divorce, but Roman law did. It is one more sign that Mark wrote with Roman readers in mind.

insights.title: Indignant for the children
insights.body: Jesus was "moved with indignation" when the disciples turned children away (10:14), an emotion only Mark reports. He takes them in his arms and blesses them (10:16). Receiving the kingdom means receiving it like a child (10:15).

insights.title: He loved him
insights.body: Only Mark says "Jesus looking at him loved him" (10:21) before telling the rich man to sell everything. The hard command comes from love. The man's face falls, and he goes away sorrowful (10:22).

insights.title: With persecutions
insights.body: Jesus promises a hundred times more houses and family now, "with persecutions" (10:30). The new family is the community of believers who share homes and lives. Only Mark adds the sober note about persecution.

insights.title: A ransom for many
insights.body: "For the Son of Man also came not to be served, but to serve, and to give his life as a ransom for many" (10:45). Many see this as the key verse of Mark. Lytron was the price that set a captive free, and for many echoes Isaiah's servant.

insights.title: Following on the way
insights.body: Bartimaeus throws off his cloak, perhaps all he owned, and once healed he "followed Jesus on the way" (10:52). The section on discipleship that began with a blind man seeing in two stages ends with a blind man seeing clearly. The way leads to Jerusalem.

insights.title: What do you want?
insights.body: Jesus asks James and John and then Bartimaeus the same question: "What do you want me to do for you?" (10:36, 10:51). The brothers ask for glory; the blind man asks for sight. What would you ask for?

11.summary: Jesus enters Jerusalem on a colt to shouts of Hosanna, curses a fig tree, clears the Temple, teaches about faith and forgiveness, and refuses to tell the leaders where his authority comes from.
11.lookfor: Notice how the fig tree story wraps around the Temple scene, the words "for all the nations", and the leaders' calculation.

names.name: Bethsphage
names.gloss: A village on the Mount of Olives (usually spelled Bethphage).

names.name: Bethany
names.gloss: A village where Jesus stayed each night.

names.name: Mount of Olives
names.gloss: The ridge east of Jerusalem.

insights.title: A colt never ridden
insights.body: Jesus asks for a colt "on which no one has sat" (11:2). Animals set apart for sacred use were to be unused, like the heifer for purification or the cows that pulled the ark. The humble king of Zechariah comes on a colt.

insights.title: The kingdom of our father David
insights.body: Only Mark has the shout, "Blessed is the kingdom of our father David that is coming" (11:10). The crowd hopes for David's kingdom restored. They sing the pilgrim words of Psalm 118.

insights.title: He looked around
insights.body: Jesus first enters the Temple, looks around at everything, and leaves because it is late (11:11). He acts the next day. The pause shows a considered decision, not a sudden outburst.

insights.title: Fig tree and Temple
insights.body: The cursing of the fig tree (11:12-14) and its withering (11:20-21) wrap around Jesus' action in the Temple (11:15-19). Each explains the other: leaves without fruit, worship without true prayer. Mark notes "it was not the season for figs" (11:13), signalling an acted parable, not a fit of temper.

insights.title: For all the nations
insights.body: Only Mark quotes Isaiah's full line, "a house of prayer for all the nations" (11:17). The trading filled the outer court, the one place where Gentiles could pray. Isaiah had promised foreigners joy in God's house.

insights.title: No shortcuts
insights.body: Jesus would not let anyone "carry a container through the temple" (11:16); people apparently used the courts as a shortcut. The Mishnah later also forbade using the Temple Mount as a shortcut. Jesus insists the place be treated as holy.

insights.title: Faith without a building
insights.body: With the Temple under judgment, Jesus points to faith in God (11:22), prayer and forgiveness (11:25). The mountain cast into the sea (11:23) may point to the Temple Mount itself. God's people will not depend on a building.

insights.title: Questions we avoid
insights.body: The leaders refuse to answer Jesus' question about John because every answer would cost them (11:31-33). Are there questions about Jesus you avoid for the same reason?

12.summary: Jesus tells the parable of the wicked tenants, answers questions about taxes, the resurrection and the greatest commandment, asks how the Messiah is David's Lord, warns about showy scribes, and praises a poor widow's gift.
12.lookfor: Notice the words used of the owner's son, the scribe who agrees with Jesus, and the contrast between the scribes and the widow.

names.name: Herodians
names.gloss: Supporters of Herod Antipas.

names.name: Caesar
names.gloss: The Roman emperor.

names.name: Sadducees
names.gloss: A priestly party that denied the resurrection.

insights.title: His beloved son
insights.body: In Mark the vineyard owner has "one, his beloved son" (12:6), the words the heavenly voice used at the baptism and transfiguration. The leaders understand the parable is aimed at them (12:12). The story foretells what they are about to do.

insights.title: Bring me a denarius
insights.body: Jesus has to ask them to bring a denarius (12:15). The coin carried Tiberius's image and a claim to divine descent, offensive to strict Jews, yet his questioners have one. He says, "Render to Caesar the things that are Caesar's, and to God the things that are God's" (12:17).

insights.title: About the Bush
insights.body: Jesus cites "the book of Moses, about the Bush" (12:26), the way people found a passage before chapters and verses existed. The Sadducees accepted only the books of Moses, so he answers from them. God is still the God of Abraham, Isaac and Jacob.

insights.title: The Shema
insights.body: Only Mark includes the opening words, "Hear, Israel, the Lord our God, the Lord is one" (12:29). This is the Shema, from the Hebrew for hear, which devout Jews recite morning and evening. Jesus joins it to love of neighbour (12:31).

insights.title: Not far from the Kingdom
insights.body: Only Mark records a scribe agreeing that love matters more than burnt offerings (12:33). Jesus tells him, "You are not far from God's Kingdom" (12:34). Not all scribes were his enemies.

insights.title: David's Lord
insights.body: Psalm 110 (12:36) was widely understood to speak of the Messiah. If David calls him Lord, he must be more than David's son. The early church used this psalm to speak of Jesus seated at God's right hand.

insights.title: Two small coins
insights.body: The widow gives "two small brass coins, which equal a quadrans coin" (12:42); a quadrans was the smallest Roman coin. Mark explains the Jewish coins by a Roman one, another sign of a Roman audience. Jesus says she gave more than all the rich (12:43).

insights.title: All she had
insights.body: The scribes "devour widows' houses" (12:40), and moments later a widow gives "all that she had to live on" (12:44). What would your giving look like if it were measured by what is left rather than by the amount?

13.summary: On the Mount of Olives Jesus tells four disciples about the Temple's destruction, persecutions, false messiahs, the coming of the Son of Man, and the need to keep watch, since no one knows the hour.
13.lookfor: Notice what must happen first, the aside to the reader, and the times of night named at the end.

names.name: Mount of Olives
names.gloss: The ridge facing the Temple.

names.name: Andrew
names.gloss: Peter's brother, one of the first four disciples.

names.name: Daniel
names.gloss: The prophet who spoke of the abomination of desolation.

names.name: Judea
names.gloss: The region around Jerusalem.

insights.title: What stones!
insights.body: A disciple marvels at the Temple's stones (13:1). Herod's builders used huge limestone blocks, some more than ten metres long, still visible in the Western Wall. Within about forty years the Temple was destroyed (13:2).

insights.title: The first four
insights.body: Peter, James, John and Andrew ask privately (13:3), the first four disciples Jesus called. This chapter is Jesus' longest speech in Mark. It prepares them for what is coming after he is gone.

insights.title: First to all nations
insights.body: Before the end, "The Good News must first be preached to all the nations" (13:10). Mission, not calculation, is the disciples' task while they wait. The Spirit will give them words when they are put on trial (13:11).

insights.title: Let the reader understand
insights.body: The aside "let the reader understand" (13:14) speaks straight to Mark's readers. If Mark wrote around the Jewish war, the warning to flee Judea for the mountains was urgent. The church historian Eusebius records that Jerusalem's Christians fled to Pella before the siege.

insights.title: Standing where it ought not
insights.body: "The abomination of desolation, spoken of by Daniel" (13:14) recalls the desecration of the Temple under Antiochus IV. Mark's Greek uses a masculine form for standing, which may point to a person rather than an object. Daniel's words found a new fulfilment.

insights.title: Nor the Son
insights.body: "But of that day or that hour no one knows, not even the angels in heaven, nor the Son, but only the Father" (13:32). Church fathers explained this as Jesus speaking from his human nature, or as knowledge he was not sent to reveal. Either way it rules out date-setting.

insights.title: Watch
insights.body: The chapter ends with one word for everyone: "Watch" (13:37), the Greek gregoreo, stay awake. The four times named in 13:35, evening, midnight, cockcrow and morning, match the next chapters: the supper, Gethsemane, Peter's denial, and the dawn trial before Pilate.

insights.title: Each one his work
insights.body: The absent master gives "to each one his work" (13:34). What work has been given to you while you wait?

14.summary: A woman anoints Jesus at Bethany and Judas agrees to betray him; Jesus eats the Passover with the Twelve and prays in Gethsemane; he is arrested while a young man flees naked, is condemned by the high priest, and is denied by Peter.
14.lookfor: Notice the woman's costly gift, how Jesus addresses God in Gethsemane, and his answer to the high priest.

names.name: Bethany
names.gloss: A village near Jerusalem.

names.name: Judas Iscariot
names.gloss: The disciple who betrayed Jesus.

names.name: Mount of Olives
names.gloss: The ridge east of Jerusalem.

names.name: Gethsemane
names.gloss: An olive grove at the foot of the Mount of Olives.

insights.title: Pure nard
insights.body: The ointment was "pure nard" (14:3), an aromatic oil from a plant of the Himalayas. It was worth "more than three hundred denarii" (14:5), about a year's wages for a labourer. She breaks the jar and holds nothing back.

insights.title: She did what she could
insights.body: Only Mark records, "She has done what she could" (14:8). The onlookers see waste; Jesus sees love and preparation for his burial. He promises she will be remembered wherever the good news is told (14:9).

insights.title: A man with a water jar
insights.body: Carrying water was usually women's work, so a man with a water jar would stand out (14:13). The arrangement suggests the meal was planned discreetly. Some have linked the upper room with the house of Mark's mother, where the church later met.

insights.title: Blood of the covenant
insights.body: "This is my blood of the new covenant, which is poured out for many" (14:24). The words recall Moses sprinkling covenant blood at Sinai and Isaiah's servant who poured out his life. Christians of every tradition trace the Lord's Supper to this meal, though they understand it differently.

insights.title: Abba
insights.body: Jesus prays, "Abba, Father" (14:36). Abba is Aramaic for father, used within families by children and adults alike. Paul says believers also cry Abba by the Spirit.

insights.title: The young man who fled
insights.body: Only Mark tells of a young man who fled naked, leaving his linen cloth behind (14:51-52). Many have guessed he was Mark himself, quietly signing his Gospel, though the text does not say. The scene shows that everyone abandoned Jesus.

insights.title: I am
insights.body: Asked whether he is the Christ, Jesus answers, "I am" (14:62), his plainest claim in Mark. He adds words from Psalm 110 and Daniel 7. The secret kept through the Gospel comes out at the moment it leads to his condemnation.

insights.title: The rooster crows twice
insights.body: Only Mark says the rooster would crow twice (14:30, 14:72). Peter warms himself at the fire and denies Jesus at the very moment Jesus confesses who he is inside (14:54, 14:62). If Mark's Gospel echoes Peter's preaching, Peter told his own failure.

15.summary: Jesus is handed over to Pilate, who releases Barabbas and has Jesus flogged and crucified; soldiers mock him, Simon of Cyrene carries his cross, Jesus dies crying out the words of Psalm 22, the Temple veil tears, a centurion confesses him, and Joseph of Arimathaea buries him.
15.lookfor: Notice the times of day, the mocking titles, and who finally calls Jesus the Son of God.

names.name: Pilate
names.gloss: Pontius Pilate, Roman governor of Judea.

names.name: Barabbas
names.gloss: An insurgent held for murder.

names.name: Praetorium
names.gloss: The governor's headquarters.

names.name: Cyrene
names.gloss: A city in North Africa with a Jewish community.

names.name: Alexander
names.gloss: A son of Simon of Cyrene, apparently known to Mark's readers.

names.name: Rufus
names.gloss: Another son of Simon of Cyrene.

names.name: Golgotha
names.gloss: The place of execution; the name means skull.

names.name: Salome
names.gloss: One of the women who followed Jesus from Galilee.

insights.title: Barabbas the rebel
insights.body: Mark says Barabbas was held with "his fellow insurgents" who had committed murder in an uprising (15:7). The custom of releasing a prisoner at the feast is not recorded outside the Gospels. The crowd chooses a violent rebel over a king who refused violence.

insights.title: Alexander and Rufus
insights.body: Simon of Cyrene is "the father of Alexander and Rufus" (15:21), names Mark's readers apparently knew. Paul greets a Rufus in the church at Rome. A burial cave in the Kidron valley, excavated in 1941, held a bone box inscribed Alexander son of Simon, possibly from a family of Cyrene.

insights.title: Wine with myrrh
insights.body: Jesus refuses "wine mixed with myrrh" (15:23), probably offered to dull the pain. Later he is given sour wine on a sponge (15:36). He faces his suffering with a clear mind.

insights.title: Hour by hour
insights.body: Mark marks the day: crucifixion at the third hour, about 9 a.m. (15:25); darkness from the sixth, noon (15:33); death at the ninth, about 3 p.m. (15:34). John places the sentencing at about the sixth hour, and scholars offer various explanations.

insights.title: Eloi, Eloi
insights.body: Jesus prays the opening line of Psalm 22 in Aramaic: "Eloi, Eloi, lama sabachthani?" (15:34). Bystanders mishear Eloi as Elijah (15:35). The psalm he begins moves from desolation to praise and to all nations turning to God.

insights.title: Truly the Son of God
insights.body: The first person in Mark to call Jesus God's Son is a Roman centurion at the cross (15:39). Mark opened by calling Jesus the Son of God, and the heavens were torn at his baptism; now the Temple veil is torn (15:38), with the same Greek verb.

insights.title: Preparation Day
insights.body: Jesus dies on "the Preparation Day, that is, the day before the Sabbath" (15:42). The Greek word, paraskeue, is still the word for Friday in Greek. Joseph of Arimathaea "boldly went in to Pilate" (15:43), risking his standing to bury a condemned man.

insights.title: Watching from afar
insights.body: The women watch from a distance (15:40-41) and see where he is laid (15:47). Where would you have stood that day?

16.summary: Women come to anoint Jesus' body and find the stone rolled away and a young man who tells them Jesus is risen; they flee in fear, and a longer ending, missing from the oldest manuscripts, adds appearances and a commission.
16.lookfor: Notice the women's worry on the way, the two words added to the message, and where the oldest manuscripts end.

names.name: Mary Magdalene
names.gloss: A follower of Jesus from Magdala.

names.name: Salome
names.gloss: One of the women at the tomb.

names.name: Galilee
names.gloss: Where the disciples are told they will see Jesus.

insights.title: Spices for the body
insights.body: The women buy spices to anoint the body (16:1), as there had been no time before the Sabbath. Anointing honoured the dead and slowed the smell of decay. On the way they worry about the stone (16:3).

insights.title: And Peter
insights.body: The young man says, "tell his disciples and Peter" (16:7). Only Mark singles out Peter, who had denied Jesus. If the Gospel echoes Peter's preaching, he remembered this word of grace.

insights.title: For they were afraid
insights.body: The oldest manuscripts end at verse 8: "They said nothing to anyone; for they were afraid." Some scholars think the original ending was lost; many now think Mark stopped here on purpose, leaving readers to answer for themselves. The promise of 16:7 assumes the disciples did meet him.

insights.title: The longer ending
insights.body: Verses 9-20 are missing from the two oldest complete manuscripts, Sinaiticus and Vaticanus, and their style differs from the rest of Mark. They gather appearances also told in Luke, John and Acts. The Catholic Church accepts them as Scripture, the Orthodox read them in worship, and most Protestant Bibles print them with a note.

insights.title: First to Mary Magdalene
insights.body: The longer ending says Jesus appeared first to Mary Magdalene, "from whom he had cast out seven demons" (16:9). Luke mentions the seven demons, and John tells of her meeting with Jesus in the garden. Those who heard her did not believe (16:11).

insights.title: To the whole creation
insights.body: "Go into all the world, and preach the Good News to the whole creation" (16:15). The good news that began beside the Sea of Galilee goes out everywhere. The book ends with the disciples preaching and the Lord working with them (16:20).

insights.title: Serpents and poison
insights.body: The signs listed (16:17-18) echo events in Acts, such as Paul surviving a viper's bite. A few groups have practised snake handling literally, sometimes with fatal results. Most Christians read these as signs that accompanied the apostles, not tests to perform, since Jesus refused to put God to the test.

insights.title: Who will roll the stone?
insights.body: The women worried about a problem God had already solved (16:3-4). What worry are you carrying toward something God may already have dealt with?

intro.who: Papias, an early second-century bishop, says Mark wrote down Peter's preaching, and tradition identifies him with John Mark of Acts. The book itself is anonymous; most scholars accept the link with Peter as possible and think Mark was the first Gospel written, used by Matthew and Luke.
intro.when: Most date it to about AD 65–70, around Nero's persecution and the Jewish war with Rome. Early tradition places it in Rome, while some scholars suggest Syria or Galilee.
intro.why: Mark tells, at breathless pace, how Jesus the Son of God came not to be served but to serve and give his life. Almost half the book covers the road to Jerusalem and the last week, and it shows the disciples' struggles honestly for readers who were suffering too.
